desc:
A town has n junctions numbered 0 to n - 1 and a set of one-way roads. Each entry roads[i] = [a, b, w] is a road from junction a to junction b that takes w minutes to drive.

Return an array dist of length n where dist[v] is the least number of minutes needed to drive from src to v, or -1 if v cannot be reached. Note that dist[src] = 0. Several roads may join the same pair of junctions and a road may even lead back to its own start.

n = 4, src = 0
roads = [[0,1,4], [0,2,1], [2,1,2], [1,3,5]]
-> [0, 3, 1, 8]

Junction 1 is reached faster through junction 2 (1 + 2 = 3) than directly (4).
hints: Breadth-first search finds fewest roads, not least minutes. You need to expand junctions in order of their travel time.
Keep the best known time to each junction. Always expand the unfinished junction with the smallest known time; use a min-heap of (time, junction) to find it.
When you pop (t, u) and t is larger than the recorded best time of u, skip it (stale entry). Otherwise relax every road u -> v with w: if t + w improves dist[v], record it and push (t + w, v).
editorial: This is Dijkstra's algorithm. Because all times are positive, the first time a junction is popped from the min-heap its time is final: any other route would have to pass through a junction that is still waiting in the heap with an equal or larger time, and adding a positive road time cannot make it smaller.

Initialise all distances to infinity except dist[src] = 0, push (0, src), and process as described in the hints. Stale heap entries are skipped by comparing the popped time with the stored best. Each road causes at most one push, so the heap holds at most E entries and the total time is O((V + E) log E). Junctions that are never reached keep infinity, which becomes -1 in the output.
Parallel roads and self-loops need no special handling: a self-loop never improves a distance (w > 0), and with parallel roads the cheaper one wins at relaxation time.
